verdict.tagline: Tough bosses and linear paths define a masterclass in dark fantasy.
for_you_if: you want precise and demanding boss encounters
you enjoy focused progression over open-world wandering
not_for_you_if: you dislike long runs back to boss arenas
you want an open map to explore freely
you intend to grind achievements across multiple playthroughs

citations.review_text:
Is it possible that you put a fucking bonfire 15 kilometers from the boss and on that way there are 3 groups of enemies between which I have to summon the tortured Gotthard who every third time reaches the arena where five people beat me at the same time, I won't even comment on the second phase.
I spent all the items, used all the souls, now it would take me 3 hours to farm and hope I'll get lucky, no way!
very fun and pretty challenging for some bosses. runbacks can be a pain in the ass. play if you liked elden ring

So far so good.
Few problems about the game in my opinion are it's difficulty do not come from hardness of the bosses, instead it mainly includes areas and some regular enemies but mostly the choices fromsoft made about the distances between bonfires, boss or regular area runbacks and map design. Having a complex/multiroute design whilst not having a map is obviously a choice. But it is just not cup of my tea. Although, they keep traveling fairly easy and understandable. And after playing Elden Ring I can easily say that exploration asset is a strong part of this game aswell and I enjoy it. (ofcourse it is limited since it is a linear game)
Overall loved the areas, general aesthetic, enemy types, the music and the similarities with Elden Ring (for example the area you defeat pontiff sulyvahn is much lookalike with the area you defeat godskin noble in volcano manor, even the elevators and their location.)
And my last complain is I did not come across a memorable boss yet. (I am aware lots of iconic bosses are    close to endgame)

single_points.text: One reviewer states that actions queued while stunned regularly resulted in death.

citation.review_text:
Upfront: I did not and do not intend to finish this game. For context, I played this immediately after completing both DS:R and DS2. However, this game's combat & puzzle-solving are simply too from enjoyable for me to continue, despite the graphical & technical quality being the series' best!

My deal-breakers were a combination of combat pacing, frustrating controls, and lackluster puzzles. First, fights against both mobs & bosses are at hyper speed compared to the series' other entries. Where a four-hit combo was a rarity in prior titles, such an attack string is the starting point for DS3. Be prepared to regularly encounter basic enemies that swing with the endurance, haste, and range of a renowned swimmer using a scoop to pummel anyone who dares try to exit the pool. Clearly it's doable, but those moments of consciousness between drownings weren't exactly making me thrilled to jump back in. Second, the controls are somehow more irritating than previous two titles– despite overall being the most refined of the series– entirely due to input queuing. This very much seems to be a case of two steps forward and one step back, because the character handles quite well, but actions queued while stunned regularly resulted in death. Third, this game's puzzles felt comparatively lackluster. I think a contributing factor is the linearity of the level design and more closed nature of the world, but either way it's disappointing. Finally, a few smaller negatives included a big disparity between the weakest mobs & (basic) attack-spammy mobs, NPCs giving too much direction on where to go, and NPC invaders & similar still being terrible experiences.

Despite my frustrations, there's a lot to enjoy about this game! Overall, I'd describe the game as a DS1 redux with the best of DS2 splashed. This game better executes concepts from DS2, such as a "vendor hub" (at the expense of flavor), faster-paced combat (not my personal preference), and minimizing platforming (terrible in eve…

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the game features a linear progression and world structure compared to earlier entries in the series.

citations.review_text:
This is one of the best games I have ever played and the first run through this game is incredible. The combat in this game is substantially better then that of dark souls 1 and 2 and still holds its place as having some of the best combat in a souls game that we have gotten. The bosses are simply incredible even though I do think that the DLC bosses are for the most part, much better. In terms of replayability, I found that it is not as replayable as dark souls 1, but this is simply because dark souls 1's map design is designed for you to not find a lot of things especially when theres optional areas and checkpoints. Not to say that this game doesn't have that, but its overall design is more linear compared to dark souls 1. If I were to compare this to many other souls like games, I would say that this one is probably one of the harder ones, though there are still many that are more difficult. 

Should you play this:
If you liked any of fromsoftwares games, you will like this one. It is simply an incredible game and even though the game is 10 years old, I would without a doubt reccomend this to anyone who is looking for a challenge.

Masterpiece, specially the boss themes as they are out standing and insane, even some better than ER best bosses, Emotional. Other aspects of the game are also beautiful the least can be said is fine.
This gamer is for people who like straight (Linear) progress games...
and yeah have fun...

Coming from Elden Ring, Dark Souls 3 actually felt more enjoyable and manageable for me. Playing as a pure Pyromancer build (spamming Chaos Bed Vestiges) is an absolute blast—bosses are challenging yet fair, with clear rhythm and punish windows. None of that blatant input-reading or relentless, dirty spamming that gives you zero room to breathe like some endgame Elden Ring bosses.

The semi-linear level design is fantastic: areas are large enough to feel rewarding to explore, yet tight and memorable enough that you won't get lost or burnt out. Going for 100% achievements was a fun challenge, though fair warning: the platinum requires NG++ to collect all 107 rings (+0, +1, +2), and NPC questlines/gestures are notoriously easy to mess up without a checklist.

Just got the 100% achievements, felt completely satisfied, and ready to retire. An absolute masterpiece that respects the player's time and patience.

Dark Souls III feels like a more refined version of the previous games in many ways. The world is dark and full of strange creatures, and exploring new areas is always interesting, especially when you discover hidden paths or uncover how certain locations connect.

The game doesn't explain much, so you often have to figure things out for yourself. I think learning from mistakes is part of the experience for many players, though paying attention to your surroundings and observing enemy behaviour can help you avoid unnecessary deaths.

The atmosphere is one of the game's strongest aspects, with the music, visuals, and environments fitting together really well. There are also plenty of references to the earlier games, especially Dark Souls Remastered. If you've played the first two games, you'll recognize familiar characters, locations, and pieces of lore, making some discoveries more meaningful.

The combat is smooth and responsive, allowing for different approaches to fights. Enemy and boss encounters are challenging, encouraging players to experiment with different strategies rather than relying on the same approach every time. The game runs mostly well on PC, with only minor slowdowns and occasional objects popping into view unexpectedly.

The world is not as fully interconnected as Dark Souls 1, with a more linear progression and a structure somewhat similar to Dark Souls 2 in some aspects. I have attached a Steam guide for players using keyboard and mouse, as I played the entire trilogy using keyboard and mouse and keyboard and mouse controls work better than Dark Souls Remastered and Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin in this game.

Even the entire Dark Souls trilogy offers hundreds of hours of gameplay with strong replayability, though the price is high even during sales, especially for games that are over a decade old. I’m not complaining, but it still seems like a concern, since the price is often similar to or even higher than newer AAA games on sale. H…

DS3 is a solid experience. It has well crafted bosses, decent (albeit linear) progression, enough build variety to remain interesting on replay and some of the best multiplayer in the soulsborne series. My main contentions moreso come with covenant grinds and trying to 100% this game's achievements. Every souls game has had grinds and obscure achievments... But those skeletons in carthus were bad enough that I ended up just pvp'ing in this largely dead game as it was still faster to do that than rely on such a tiny drop pool. 

Still, that's a very niche gripe - if you enjoyed the other souls games and are looking for something a bit faster paced with some darker fantasy tropes then this game is definitely for you.

Dark Souls 3 was my first Souls game. I got through the main game pretty smoothly—except for Nameless King. Truly the Sun's Firstborn; it took me a whole afternoon to beat him. And this DLC is even more putrid—extreme numbers, pure stat-checking.
  So I only finished the DLC on my first playthrough and never touched it on later cycles—especially Sister Friede. After beating her second phase I'd put on the Symbol of Avarice, then awkwardly took it off, only for a third phase to start, so I scrambled to put the Symbol back on. But the DLC did have its bright spot: Slave Knight Gael, Grandpa Gael. He's tanky, sure, but his moves are all big, wide, open swings, so rolling against him feels incredibly smooth.
  And when going for 100% achievements, the worst part was farming covenant items—especially the Proof of a Concord Kept and Vertebra Shackle. I'd recommend equipping the Symbol of Avarice, Gold Serpent Ring +3, and the Crystal Sage's Rapier, pop a Rusted Coin, and go farm. Once the covenant item drops, just reload the area and farm again.

One of the best games ever made. 

It is easy to forget this game with Elden Ring now made, but this game stands as a titan in it's own right. You will find few people who glaze Elden Ring more than me, but despite that; Dark Souls 3 does several things as good, and even better, than Elden Ring. 

If you are coming here from Elden Ring, keep 1 thing in mind: 
-Dark Souls 3, in comparison to Elden Ring, is far, far more linear. This means, that if you hit a roadblock and a hurdle that you struggle getting past, you cannot leave to go explore elsewhere, and return 14 hours later to then easily defeat the boss once you have gotten stronger. 

When you hit a roadblock here, you are pretty much stuck here, with a few exceptions, until you defeat it. 

Still, if you enjoyed the difficulty of Elden Ring and are curious about the other Souls games; I cannot recommend DS3 enough. This game will forever have a deep, personal and special place in my heart until the day i die.

single_points.text: One reviewer states that players still get knocked around by the first enemies in the game no matter the armor setup.

citation.review_text: I really love this game but it's not my favorite Soulsborne. The environments, the lore, the weapon skill system, a lot of the bosses are fun and cool and flashy. My main complaint is how they changed the poise system from DS1&2 in this. It's frustrating to still be getting knocked around like a cat batting at a rubber mouse by the first enemies in the game no matter your armor setup or level. Even after "getting used to it" it still makes me rage occasionally when I get ultra combo'd by super weak enemies as I run through early areas at a much higher level to look for items i missed.

single_points.text: One reviewer states that if you are not on controller it is going to suck.

citation.review_text:
I got into souls-like games with DS2 SOTFS for christmas 2014 thanks to my dad, one of the hardest games I ever played up till that point. I spent 400 hours my first playthrough and I love/hated every second of it. 

I wanted to play DS3 cause of PewDiePie's lets-play series cause I thought the game looked really cool and I was playing Infinity Blade 1&2 when it was still on mobile stores and kept thinking on if I should get DS3. 

DS3 was really fun to play, my main gripes is not being able to hyperfixate on jumping randomly all the time(3D platformer habits), yellow color themes(Elden Ring has this too), and being too metallic and shiny though I can praise the sun since modders have fixed this issue. 

I love the look of Lords of The Fallen, they have a great color design with their game, Nightreign kind of gives me that vibe and I enjoyed solo expeditions in Nightreign. 

Is DS3 worth playing in 2026? Short Answer: If you have the patience. 

Is DS3 worth playing in 2026?: This is a pre-covid, non-vibe coded, non brainrot produced game. You're going to suffer, it's hard, if you're not on controller it's going to suck shit, if you want to play a game that is worth the grind then pick up a controller and prepare to ALMOST smash it a few times.
